question: In A Study in Scarlet, who first told Watson about Sherlock Holmes, where did the two of them run into each other, and why did he think Watson and Holmes might suit each other?
verified:
It was young Stamford, who had been a dresser under Watson at Barts. Watson ran into him at the Criterion Bar and took him to lunch at the Holborn. When Watson said he was looking for lodgings, Stamford told him about a man working at the chemical laboratory at the hospital who wanted someone to go halves with him in rooms that were too much for his purse. That man was Sherlock Holmes, and Stamford took Watson to the laboratory and introduced them.

Evidence (verbatim):
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:2] "I was standing at the Criterion Bar, when some one tapped me on the shoulder, and turning round I recognized young Stamford, who had been a dresser under me at Barts."
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:2] "I asked him to lunch with me at the Holborn"
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:3] "A fellow who is working at the chemical laboratory up at the hospital."
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:4] "If you like, we shall drive round together after luncheon."
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:3] "he could not get someone to go halves with him in some nice rooms which he had found, and which were too much for his purse."
- [05ab674df048d13f:5:6] "Dr. Watson, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” said Stamford, introducing us."

question: At the scene of the first murder in each novel, Holmes describes the wanted man to the police before anyone has caught him. What does he say about the murderer in A Study in Scarlet, and whom does he name and describe in The Sign of the Four?
verified:
In A Study in Scarlet, at Lauriston Gardens, Holmes tells Gregson and Lestrade that the murderer was a man more than six feet high, in the prime of life, with small feet for his height. He wore coarse, square-toed boots and smoked a Trichinopoly cigar. He came with his victim in a four-wheeled cab drawn by a horse with three old shoes and one new one on its off fore leg. He probably had a florid face, and the finger-nails of his right hand were remarkably long. In The Sign of the Four, at Pondicherry Lodge, Holmes gives Athelney Jones the name Jonathan Small. He describes him as poorly educated, small and active, with his right leg off and a wooden stump worn away on the inner side. His left boot has a coarse, square-toed sole with an iron band round the heel. He is middle-aged, much sunburned and a former convict, and a good deal of skin is missing from the palm of his hand.

- [05ab674df048d13f:7:15] "In all probability the murderer had a florid face, and the finger-nails of his right hand were remarkably long."

question: In each novel a feeble-looking old person turns up at Baker Street who is really someone in disguise. Who was in disguise in each book, what did they pretend to be, and how was the disguise found out?
verified:
In A Study in Scarlet a very old, wrinkled woman calling herself Mrs. Sawyer answers Holmes's advertisement for the found ring. She claims it belongs to her daughter, whose married name is Dennis (she married Tom Dennis), and gives her address as 13, Duncan Street, Houndsditch. Holmes rides behind her four-wheeler, but when it arrives the cab is empty. No. 13 belongs to a paperhanger named Keswick, and nobody there has heard of Sawyer or Dennis. Holmes concludes it must have been a young, active man and an incomparable actor. Jefferson Hope later says only that his friend volunteered to go, and never names him. In The Sign of the Four the disguised man is Holmes himself, dressed as an aged man in seafaring garb with an old pea-jacket. He claims to know where Mordecai Smith's boat, the men and the treasure are. He fools both Watson and Athelney Jones, then reveals himself by holding out the wig, whiskers and eyebrows. He explains that the criminal classes are beginning to know him, so he can only work under a disguise.

- [05ab674df048d13f:9:6] "13, Duncan Street, Houndsditch. A weary way from here."
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:6] "Sally will be a glad woman this night. That’s the ring."
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:6] "My name is Sawyer—hers is Dennis, which Tom Dennis married her"
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:9] "having seen her safely inside, I perched myself behind."
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:9] "Nothing came out though."
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:9] "On inquiring at Number 13 we found that the house belonged to a respectable paperhanger, named Keswick, and that no one of the name either of Sawyer or Dennis had ever been heard of there."
- [05ab674df048d13f:9:11] "It must have been a young man, and an active one, too, besides being an incomparable actor."
- [05ab674df048d13f:17:17] "My friend volunteered to go and see. I think you’ll own he did it smartly."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:12:10] "He was an aged man, clad in seafaring garb, with an old pea-jacket buttoned up to his throat."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:12:11] "Was it about Mordecai Smith’s boat?” “Yes. I knows well where it is. An’ I knows where the men he is after are."

- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:12:12] "a good many of the criminal classes begin to know me,—especially since our friend here took to publishing some of my cases: so I can only go on the war-path under some simple disguise like this."

question: After Brigham Young gave Lucy Ferrier a month to choose a husband, how was John Ferrier reminded each day of how much time he had left?
verified:
Each morning his unseen enemies marked up how many days of the month of grace were left. First he found a small square of paper pinned to the coverlet of his bed, just over his chest, reading "Twenty-nine days are given you for amendment, and then——". The next morning the number 28 was scrawled on the ceiling, apparently with a burned stick. The morning after that, a great 27 was painted on the outside of his door. After that the numbers kept appearing on the walls, on the floors, and on small placards stuck on the garden gate or the railings. Ferrier never found out where they came from.

- [05ab674df048d13f:15:5] "With all his vigilance John Ferrier could not discover whence these daily warnings proceeded."

question: When Jefferson Hope led the Ferriers out of Salt Lake City, how did they get past the sentinel in the mountain pass, and how had Hope learned what to say?
verified:
Challenged with "Who goes there?", Hope answered "Travellers for Nevada". Asked by whose permission, Ferrier said "The Holy Four". The sentinel then cried "Nine from seven", and Hope answered "Seven from five", so the sentinel let them pass. Hope knew the countersign because earlier that night, while the three of them lay hidden by the gap into the cornfields, he had overheard two Mormon watchers arrange a meeting and part with a sign and countersign ("Nine to seven!" / "Seven to five!").

question: Trace Jefferson Hope's pursuit of Drebber and Stangerson after they left Utah. Why had they left, where in America did he find them and what happened to him there, and which European cities did he follow them through?
verified:
Drebber and Stangerson had left Utah in a schism, when some younger members rebelled against the Elders and left. Hope travelled from town to town in the United States for years until he glimpsed a face in a window and knew they were in Cleveland, Ohio. Drebber recognised him in the street and went with Stangerson, now his private secretary, to a justice of the peace, claiming they were in danger of their lives from an old rival. Hope was taken into custody and, unable to find sureties, was held for some weeks. By the time he was released they had left for Europe. He followed them to St. Petersburg, but they had left for Paris. In Paris he learned they had gone to Copenhagen, and there he was again a few days late because they had gone on to London, where he finally caught up with them.

- [05ab674df048d13f:16:13] "the result had been the secession of a certain number of the malcontents, who had left Utah and become Gentiles. Among these had been Drebber and Stangerson"
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:13] "that one glance told him that Cleveland in Ohio possessed the men whom he was in pursuit of."
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:13] "some of the younger members of the Church having rebelled against the authority of the Elders"
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:14] "He hurried before a justice of the peace, accompanied by Stangerson, who had become his private secretary, and represented to him that they were in danger of their lives from the jealousy and hatred of an old rival."
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:14] "That evening Jefferson Hope was taken into custody, and not being able to find sureties, was detained for some weeks."
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:14] "Drebber’s house was deserted, and that he and his secretary had departed for Europe."
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:14] "When he reached St. Petersburg they had departed for Paris; and when he followed them there he learned that they had just set off for Copenhagen."
- [05ab674df048d13f:16:14] "At the Danish capital he was again a few days late, for they had journeyed on to London, where he at last succeeded in running them to earth."

question: How did Jefferson Hope get into the empty house in the Brixton Road where he killed Drebber?
verified:
He had a duplicate key. Some days earlier, a gentleman who had been looking over some houses in the Brixton Road dropped the key of one of them in Hope's cab. It was claimed and returned that same evening, but in the meantime Hope took a moulding of it and had a duplicate made. That gave him at least one place in London where he could count on not being interrupted.

Evidence (verbatim):

- [05ab674df048d13f:17:7] "It was claimed that same evening, and returned; but in the interval I had taken a moulding of it, and had a duplicate constructed."
- [05ab674df048d13f:17:8] "By means of this I had access to at least one spot in this great city where I could rely upon being free from interruption."

question: In A Study in Scarlet, how did Holmes learn the name of the man who killed Drebber, and what had Gregson failed to ask?
verified:
Holmes telegraphed the head of the police at Cleveland and asked only about the circumstances of Enoch Drebber's marriage. The ring found at the scene had convinced him the murderer was reminding his victim of some dead or absent woman. The reply said that Drebber had already applied for the protection of the law against an old rival in love named Jefferson Hope, and that Hope was at present in Europe. Gregson had also telegraphed Cleveland, but he only described the circumstances and asked about Stangerson. He did not ask about any particular point in Drebber's former career.

- [05ab674df048d13f:18:4] "Clearly the murderer had used it to remind his victim of some dead or absent woman."
- [05ab674df048d13f:18:5] "I telegraphed to the head of the police at Cleveland, limiting my enquiry to the circumstances connected with the marriage of Enoch Drebber."
- [05ab674df048d13f:18:5] "It told me that Drebber had already applied for the protection of the law against an old rival in love, named Jefferson Hope, and that this same Hope was at present in Europe."

- [05ab674df048d13f:7:11] "“I asked about Stangerson.”"
- [05ab674df048d13f:7:11] "“Have you sent to Cleveland?” “We telegraphed this morning.”"
- [05ab674df048d13f:18:4] "I asked Gregson whether he had enquired in his telegram to Cleveland as to any particular point in Mr. Drebber’s former career. He answered, you remember, in the negative."

question: In The Sign of the Four, how did Mary Morstan come to receive a pearl every year, who was sending them, and where did the pearls come from?
verified:
On 4 May 1882 an advertisement in the Times asked for Miss Mary Morstan's address. On her employer's advice she published it in the advertisement column. The same day a small card-board box arrived by post containing a large, lustrous pearl, with no letter, and a similar box came every year on the same date. She showed Holmes and Watson six of them. Thaddeus Sholto later explains that the pearls were taken from a chaplet of pearls from the Agra treasure that his father, Major Sholto, had got out intending to send to her. Thaddeus persuaded his brother Bartholomew to let him find Miss Morstan's address and send her a detached pearl at fixed intervals, so that she might never feel destitute.

Evidence (verbatim):
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:3] "upon the 4th of May, 1882—an advertisement appeared in the Times asking for the address of Miss Mary Morstan"
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:3] "By her advice I published my address in the advertisement column."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:3] "The same day there arrived through the post a small card-board box addressed to me, which I found to contain a very large and lustrous pearl."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:3] "Since then every year upon the same date there has always appeared a similar box, containing a similar pearl, without any clue as to the sender."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:4] "showed me six of the finest pearls that I had ever seen."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:7:13] "We could judge the splendour of the missing riches by the chaplet which he had taken out."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:7:7] "See that chaplet dipped with pearls beside the quinine-bottle. Even that I could not bear to part with, although I had got it out with the design of sending it to her."

question: In The Sign of the Four, what did the anonymous letter tell Mary Morstan to do, and who was the man who met her party at the rendezvous?
verified:
The letter told her to be at the third pillar from the left outside the Lyceum Theatre at seven o'clock that night. She could bring two friends if she was distrustful, but must not bring the police. At the third pillar a small, dark, brisk man dressed as a coachman accosted them. He made her give her word that neither of her companions was a police-officer, then mounted the box of a four-wheeler and drove them off. Thaddeus Sholto later identifies him: Williams, one of the two prize-fighters his father employed as porters at Pondicherry Lodge, once light-weight champion of England.

Evidence (verbatim):
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:5] "Be at the third pillar from the left outside the Lyceum Theatre to-night at seven o’clock. If you are distrustful, bring two friends."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:5:5] "Do not bring police."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:6:5] "a small, dark, brisk man in the dress of a coachman accosted us."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:6:5] "I was to ask you to give me your word that neither of your companions is a police-officer."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:6:5] "He gave a shrill whistle, on which a street Arab led across a four-wheeler and opened the door."

According to Thaddeus Sholto, his father had a marked aversion to men with wooden legs and once actually fired his revolver at a wooden-legged man who turned out to be a harmless tradesman canvassing for orders. question: In Jonathan Small's story, who was the merchant Achmet and why was he going to the fort at Agra, how was he killed, and how was the murder discovered?
verified:
Achmet was a trusty servant of a rajah in the northern provinces, travelling under the guise of a merchant. The rajah wanted to be safe whichever side won the Mutiny. He kept his gold and silver in his palace vaults and sent his most precious stones and choicest pearls in an iron box to lie in the fort at Agra. When Achmet ran from his escort inside the fort, Small threw his firelock between his legs and tripped him, and a Sikh stabbed him twice in the side. They buried him under loose bricks in a crumbling hall. But the rajah had set a second, even more trusty servant to spy on Achmet. This man saw him enter the fort and later found no trace of him. He told a sergeant of guides, who told the commandant. A search found the body, and all four men were tried for murder.

question: How did Jonathan Small win Tonga's loyalty, what part did Tonga play in Small's escape from the Andaman Islands, and how did the two of them earn a living once they reached England?
verified:
Tonga was a little Andaman Islander whom a convict-gang found sick to death in the woods. Small, who had picked up some medicine, took him in hand while Dr. Somerton was down with a fever. After a couple of months he had Tonga well and able to walk, and Tonga took a fancy to him and was always hanging about his hut. Tonga was a fine boatman with a big, roomy canoe of his own. He brought it round at night to an old, unguarded wharf to pick Small up, and they escaped to sea in it. In England, Small earned their living by exhibiting Tonga at fairs and similar places as "the black cannibal". Tonga would eat raw meat and dance his war-dance, and they always collected a hatful of pennies.

- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:15:34] "One day when Dr. Somerton was down with a fever a little Andaman Islander was picked up by a convict-gang in the woods. He was sick to death, and had gone to a lonely place to die."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:15:34] "I took him in hand, though he was as venomous as a young snake, and after a couple of months I got him all right and able to walk."

- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:15:36] "I made for the boat, and in an hour we were well out at sea."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:15:37] "some three or four years ago, we found ourselves in England."
- [0ee225a9a3b5fbc2:15:38] "We earned a living at this time by my exhibiting poor Tonga at fairs and other such places as the black cannibal."
